ABSTRACT Background The kynurenine pathway (KP) plays a pivotal role in many diseases that involve distinct pathological mechanisms. Objectives Since KP metabolites are potential disease biomarkers, it is crucial to investigate their fluctuations under physiological conditions. As the KP is stress‐responsive, this study examines how peripheral KP metabolites change with core temperature increases induced by two different modalities. Methods In this randomized cross‐over study, 11 young healthy males were subjected to (a) exogenous heating via hot water immersion (44°C, EXO), and (b) exertional heating via exercise (EXE), until rectal temperature ( T rec ) reached 39°C, followed by a recovery phase. Blood samples were collected at baseline and at every 0.5°C T rec increment during both the heating and recovery phases. Plasma levels of KP metabolites, stress, and metabolic markers were measured. Correlation analyses between kynurenine pathway metabolites and stress markers were computed over the course of the trials. Results EXE and EXO trials induced the KP, but to different extents. Most plasma KP metabolite concentrations (kynurenic acid, picolinic acid, 3‐hydrokynurenine, quinolinic acid) increased. Stress markers were elevated in both trials. Changes in KP metabolites, stress, and metabolic markers were not persistent, and returned to baseline following recovery. Funding: This work was supported by grants from the Vetenskapsrådet (2024‐02812), the Hjärnfonden (FO2022‐0140), Åhlén‐stiftelsen and the Initiative for Excellence in Universities Science and Sport Lithuania (No. S‐A‐UEI‐23‐2). 1 Introduction The kynurenine pathway (KP) is the primary route of tryptophan (TRP) degradation, generating physiologically active metabolites with diverse functions. While KP in the brain primarily originates from astrocytes, its peripheral activity is mainly localized in the liver and skeletal muscles. Metabolites produced along this pathway are increasingly recognized for their roles in neurological and psychiatric disorders, as well as playing a role in immune responses, cardiovascular function, and energy metabolism [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ]. Metabolites such as kynurenine (KYN), kynurenic acid (KYNA), quinolinic acid (QUIN), and picolinic acid (PIC) have been proposed as biomarkers for tracking disease severity and progression across various conditions [ 5 , 6 ]. Understanding the regulation of this pathway in healthy individuals, both at rest and under physiological stress, is essential for assessing its dysfunction in disease states. Physiological stressors such as exercise and caloric restriction have been shown to induce the KP, with cortisol identified as a trigger in this regard [ 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 ]. Heat exposure, a universal physiological stressor, triggers thermoregulatory mechanisms and activates both neuronal and physiological processes [ 11 ]. Heat stress can be induced through exertional (EXE) means, such as exercise, which raises body temperature through muscle contraction and increased metabolic rates [ 12 ], or through exogenous (EXO) methods like hot‐water immersion [ 13 ]. Hot‐water immersion, a passive technique, is frequently used in both research and clinical settings to raise core body temperature without mechanical strain [ 12 , 13 , 14 ]. Even slight increases in core temperature are thought to provoke a modest, but rapid, inflammatory response [ 15 , 16 ]. In addition to passive heating, exercise also produces stress‐induced immune activation, but with a more pronounced response [ 17 , 18 ]. In parallel, ample evidence indicates the activation of the kynurenine pathway by exercise or infection [ 7 , 8 , 9 , 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 , 23 ]. From a functional perspective, if an increase in body temperature alone is a sufficient component to activate the KP, this could offer therapeutic potential for managing diseases involving dysregulation of the KP. It is well‐established that heat stress involves activation of both the sympathetic nervous system (SNS) and the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis. The SNS provides rapid adaptation to stressors through the release of catecholamines such as noradrenaline and adrenaline [ 24 ]. This response increases heart rate and redistributes blood flow to promote sweating and the regulation of body temperature. In contrast, the HPA axis triggers slower mechanisms involving cortisol production [ 25 ]. These responses are critical as both catecholamines and cortisol profoundly influence metabolism and immune functions, thereby impacting KP, especially under physiological stress [ 7 , 9 , 10 , 26 ]. While the majority of research on KP has been focused on its role in pathophysiological states [ 2 , 3 , 27 , 28 , 29 , 30 ], relatively few studies have examined its regulation in healthy individuals, and among these, the majority have examined how exercise influences KP metabolites [ 9 , 10 , 31 , 32 ]. This study is the first to examine the effects of core temperature elevation on KP metabolites in healthy males. More specifically, the aim is to investigate the effects of two distinct heat stress modalities on KP metabolites. Additionally, we aim to examine whether well‐established stress markers would indirectly reflect the KP kinetics observed during the different heat stress modalities. To capture any delayed effects that might emerge post‐heating, samples were also collected during the recovery phase. We hypothesize that both passive heating and a rise in body temperature due to exercise will initiate a stress response, affecting the concentration of KP metabolites. We expect the EXE trial to produce more pronounced effects due to the additional cardiovascular, mechanical, and metabolic demands associated with exercise. Specifically, EXE uniquely activates skeletal muscle, a major source of peripheral KYNA, which should lead to higher plasma KYNA levels [ 8 , 32 ] than EXO. Additionally, we hypothesize that other biomarkers, such as catecholamines, will be particularly affected in the EXE trial and may parallel changes in KP metabolites, while prolactin levels are expected to be more responsive in the EXO trial due to its sensitivity to skin temperature [ 33 ].

MNL‐SVA(M)‐2021‐331) and the Swedish Ethical Review Authority for Human Research (Dnr: 2021‐06966‐01) conducted according to the Declaration of Helsinki guidelines. A written informed consent was obtained from all subjects during the initial visit. The trial was registered at http://clinicaltrials.gov (No. NCT07064512). 2.2 Participants Eleven healthy young males were recruited for this randomized cross‐over design study (Table 1 ). Inclusion criteria were: age between 18 and 36 years, healthy status, and being physically active (exercising 2–3 times per week). Participants were excluded if they were smokers, on medication, or had a body mass index (BMI) > 30 kg/m 2 , asthma, neurological conditions, cardiovascular disease, or any condition that could be adversely affected by core temperature elevation. Additionally, the participants could not have been involved in any temperature manipulation (cold/heat acclimation) program in the 3‐month period prior to the study.

Additionally, the participants could not have been involved in any temperature manipulation (cold/heat acclimation) program in the 3‐month period prior to the study. 2.3 Experimental Protocol and Study Design Participants attended three laboratory sessions during the course of this study. To minimize the influence of prior physical activity, they were instructed to abstain from exercise for at least 48 h before each trial. To control circadian variations, all experiments began between 9:00 and 10:00 a.m. During the first visit, participants underwent a maximal incremental cycling test on an electromechanically braked cycling ergometer (Ergometrics–800S; Ergoline Medical Measurement Systems, Bitz, Germany) to determine their maximal oxygen consumption (VO 2 max). The ambient temperature in the laboratory was controlled and maintained at 23°C (humidity 40% ± 3%) during the test. This test was slightly modified based on the protocol previously described [ 34 ]. Following a warm‐up of 10 min at 50 W and a 2‐min rest, the participants began the maximal incremental test by cycling at 40 W for 4 min. Then, the power increased by 5 W every 10 s until exhaustion. Participants were required to maintain a pedaling cadence between 70 and 75 rpm. Participants breathed through a low‐resistance mouthpiece, and O 2 consumption and CO 2 production were measured breath by breath using a wireless portable gas analyzer (Oxycon Mobile; Jaeger, Hoechberg, Germany). Heart rate (HR) was determined using an HR monitor (S‐635X, Polar Electro, Kempele, Finland). Participants received verbal encouragement throughout the test. Upon the second instance of cadence dropping below 70 rpm, exhaustion was declared, and the test was concluded. Participants were considered to have reached their VO 2 max when at least three of the following criteria were attained: (1) HR reached at least 90% predicted maximal HR (220‐age), (2) respiratory exchange ratio (RER) exceeded 1.1, (3) VO 2 did not further increase during the subsequent 30 s of the test, and (4) the rated perceived exertion (RPE) reached at least 19 on the BORG (6–20 RPE) scale. VO 2 max was calculated as the highest VO 2 value over a 15‐s period and was then used to set the submaximal intensity (60% of VO 2 max) for the prolonged cycling exercise in the exertional heating modality (EXE). A summary of the participants' exercise test outcomes is shown in Table 1 . In the second and third visits, participants completed the two experimental trials: EXE or EXO as illustrated in Figure 1 . A minimum recovery period of 1 week was maintained between trials. For both the EXE and EXO trials, participants were instructed to fast for 12 h overnight. Upon arrival at the laboratory, each participant self‐inserted a rectal probe (Ellab, Hvidovre, Denmark; accuracy, ±0.01°C) to a depth of 12 cm beyond the anal sphincter. A Polar H10 chest strap (Polar H10, Polar Electro Oy, Kempele, Finland) was placed for heart rate recording, and a 20‐gauge, 32‐mm intravenous catheter was inserted into the right antecubital vein. Rectal temperature presents the gold standard of monitoring core temperature. Then, the participant was asked to rest in a semi‐recumbent position for 20 min in a quiet room at an ambient temperature of 23°C ± 0.5°C with 40% ± 3% relative humidity, and capillary lactate and glucose were measured, and blood and saliva samples were collected. Participants wore only light athletic shorts during the trial. While water intake was allowed before the start of each trial, neither food nor water were permitted during the trial. The two heating protocols were designed to achieve a comparable increase in rectal temperature ( T rec ) to 39°C within a similar timeframe, without inducing extreme heat stress. Each participant performed a standardized warm‐up of 10 min at a power output of 50 W, followed by 2 min of idle sitting before the trial began. Subsequently, the participant (baseline T rec = 37.5°C ± 0.1°C) cycled at an intensity that was defined as the power eliciting 60% VO 2 max as determined using the participant's power‐VO 2 relationship obtained during the maximal incremental test. Participants were motivated to maintain a 70‐rpm pedaling cadence during the entire trial period. The cycling exercise continued at this intensity until T rec reached 39°C. Upon reaching a T rec of 39°C, participants stopped cycling and moved to an adjacent room to rest passively on a standard chair (23°C ± 0.5°C, relative humidity of 40% ± 3%) until T rec fell to 37.5°C. Blood and saliva samples were collected, and capillary glucose and lactate were measured at each 0.5°C T rec increase up to 39°C and thereafter at each 0.5°C T rec decrease till 37.5°C. 2.5 EXO Trial Hot‐water immersion was used as the exogenous heating modality, where the participants (baseline T rec = 37.5°C ± 0.1°C) sat immersed (up to the waistline in a water bath at 44°C ± 0.5°C) and remained submerged until T rec reached 39°C. Thereafter, participants exited the bath, towel‐dried, and sat passively on a standard chair until their T rec value returned to 37.5°C. Water was maintained at the same temperature during the trial. The room temperature during the trial was 23°C ± 0.5°C. Analogously to EXE, blood samples and saliva samples were taken, and capillary glucose and lactate were measured at each 0.5°C T rec increment to 39°C and till return to 37.5°C.

Analogously to EXE, blood samples and saliva samples were taken, and capillary glucose and lactate were measured at each 0.5°C T rec increment to 39°C and till return to 37.5°C. 2.6 Serum Sample Preparation Venous blood samples from the median antecubital for measurement of serum prolactin concentration were collected directly into a 3.5 mL vacutainer tube containing silica clot activator and polymer gel for serum separation (Becton Dickinson, Franklin Lakes, NJ, USA). Serum‐separating tubes were allowed to clot for 30–60 min at room temperature, and the tubes were centrifuged at 2000 × g for 15 min at 4°C. After centrifugation, blood samples were transferred into 1.5 mL microtubes (FL Medical, Italy), and the serum microtubes were stored at −80°C until analysis. 2.7 Plasma Sample Preparation Venous blood samples were taken from the median antecubital vein into 3 mL vacutainer tubes containing tripotassium ethylenediamine tetraacetic acid as an anticoagulant (EDTA‐K3; Beckton Dickinson, Plymouth, UK), inverted 8–10 times, and kept at 2°C–8°C until centrifugation. Plasma was separated by centrifugation at 1200 × g for 15 min at 4°C within 30 min of blood collection and stored in 0.5 mL aliquots at −80°C until analysis. 2.8 Plasma Preparation for UPLC – MS / MS Thirty μl of human plasma sample, quality control or standard mix, was mixed with 30 μL of internal standard 0.5 μM in 3.2% ammonia for 15 s. After the addition of 60 μL of 200 nM ZnSO4 (5°C), the solution was mixed for 15 s. Next, 30 μL of methanol was added (5°C) and mixed for 15 s. The mixture was centrifuged for 10 min at 2841 × g , room temperature. Thirty μL of the supernatant was mixed with 30 μL of 5% formic acid in LC–MS Certified Clear Glass 12 × 32‐mm vials (product no. 186005662CV, Waters, Milford, Massachusetts, USA) before transferring the samples to an autosampler (5°C). An injection volume of 1.5 μL was used.

An injection volume of 1.5 μL was used. 2.9 Detection of TRP and KP Metabolites in Plasma Blinded assessors operated a UPLC-MS/MS system to measure plasma levels of TRP, KYN, KYNA, 3‐HK, PIC, QUIN, and NAM. The UPLC–MS/MS system used a Xevo TQ–XS triple quadrupole mass spectrometer (Waters) with a Z‐spray electrospray interface and was operated in electrospray positive multiple reaction monitoring mode. UPLC conditions: separation was carried out using an Acquity UPLC HSS T3 column (1.8 μm, 2.1 × 150 mm, Waters, part number: 186003540) at 50°C with a guard column (Waters, Vanguard HSS T3 1.8 μm, 2.1 × 50 mm column, part number: 186003976) to retain mobile phase impurities. 0.6% formic acid in water (UPLC grade) and 0.6% formic acid in methanol (UPLC grade) made up the mobile phase that ran at a 0.3 mL/min flow rate. The MS was operating at a source temperature of 150°C. The capillary voltage was set to 0.4 kV. The cone gas flow was 150 L/h and the desolvation gas flow rate was 900 L/h, while the desolvation temperature was 600°C. The autosampler was set at 5°C and the run time for each sample was 13.0 min. All metabolites measured were detected in higher concentrations than the lowest level of quantification (TRP, 5 μM; KYN, 50 nM; KYNA, 5 nM; 3‐HK, 5 nM; PIC, 5 nM; QUIN, 50 nM; and NAM, 50 nM). The coefficient of variation (CV) for quality controls (intra‐assay, during 15 h) was less than 9% for all metabolites measured. Data processing and acquisition were performed using the software package MassLynx v 4.1 SCN943 SCN979 (2016 Waters Inc.). 2.10 Plasma Stress Hormones, Serum Prolactin, and Capillary Glucose and Lactate Concentrations Plasma concentrations of adrenaline and noradrenaline were determined using an ELISA kit (CatCombi ELISA kit, RE59242 IBL International GmbH, Hamburg, Germany). Serum concentration of prolactin was determined using an ELISA kit (Prolactin ELISA kit, RE52131, IBL International GmbH). For the analysis of catecholamines and prolactin, samples were loaded in duplicates and plasma/serum concentration was determined via spectrophotometry (Spark multimode microplate reader, Tecan, Grödig, Austria). The intra‐assay CVs were 2.01%, 5.91%, and 4.59%, and the inter‐assay CVs were 2.02%, 7.12%, and 4.48% for plasma adrenaline and noradrenaline and serum prolactin, respectively. Salivary cortisol was measured in duplicates using enzyme‐linked immunosorbent assay kits (salivary free cortisol: Cat. No. RE52611, IBL International GmbH, Hamburg, Germany) and a Spark multimode microplate reader (Tecan, Grödig, Austria). The intra‐assay CV for salivary free cortisol was 2.94% and the inter‐assay CV was 8.79%. 2.13 Statistical Analysis Data were analyzed using repeated measures two‐way ANOVA followed by post hoc Dunnett's multiple comparisons test for pairwise comparisons between baseline values and all later timepoints (every 0.5°C increment). Data normality was assessed using the Shapiro–Wilk test and visual inspection of Q‐Q plots, residual plots, and histograms, while the assumption of homogeneity of variance was assessed visually. In the case of failure to pass the Shapiro–Wilk test, the data were log 2 transformed. These statistical analyses were performed in Prism (version 10.1.1; GraphPad). Correlation over time analyses for each trial were performed using the R programming language (RStudio version 2025.05.0 + 496, RStudio Team, Boston, MA, USA). Pairwise Spearman correlation ρ values between each stress marker and KP metabolite for each timepoint in each trial were calculated using the corr.test function from the psych R package. All graphs were created in Prism (version 10.1.1; GraphPad). Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. Data are presented as the mean and standard error of the mean (SEM).

Data are presented as the mean and standard error of the mean (SEM). 3 Results The time required to reach T rec increment or decrement to set point was similar in both trials (Figure 2 ), signifying an analogous timeline of heat stress exposure in each trial. Changes in physiological parameters such as lactate, prolactin levels, and heart rate were observed during both trials (Figure 3 ). As expected, lactate levels increased only upon EXE and peaked at 39°C ( p < 0.01, Figure 3B ). While prolactin levels increased upon both EXE and EXO, peaked at 39°C ( p < 0.01, Figure 3C ), and returned to baseline, the greatest increase was seen upon EXO. Conversely, glucose levels did not significantly change during either EXE or EXO (Figure 3A ). An increase in heart rate in the heating phase and return to baseline upon normalization of body temperature was observed in both trials ( p < 0.0001, Figure 3D ). Regarding heat stress parameters, the PSI dynamics were similar in both trials, while a greater increase in PSI was observed upon EXE ( p < 0.0001, Figure 3E ). In both trials, adrenaline and noradrenaline levels peaked at 39°C (EXE: p < 0.01 and p < 0.001, EXO: p < 0.05 and p > 0.05 respectively, Figure 3F,G ) and returned to baseline levels at 37.5°C baseline temperature. However, in the EXO trial, the increase in noradrenaline was smaller and not significant ( p > 0.05), whereas the increase in adrenaline was greater and statistically significant ( p < 0.05). Cortisol levels also increased in response to both EXE and EXO trials but reached peak concentrations in the recovery phase of the trials ( p < 0.001 for EXE at 38°C and p < 0.01 for EXO at 38.5°C, Figure 3H ).

Cortisol levels also increased in response to both EXE and EXO trials but reached peak concentrations in the recovery phase of the trials ( p < 0.001 for EXE at 38°C and p < 0.01 for EXO at 38.5°C, Figure 3H ). The influence of both temperature‐elevating interventions on KP metabolites was examined by measuring plasma concentrations of TRP, KYN, KYNA, QUIN, 3‐HK, PIC, and NAM, as shown in Figure 4 . Plasma TRP concentration remained stable during the heating phase of both trials but exhibited a slight significant decrease upon return to baseline temperature in the EXO trial ( p < 0.05). KYN exhibited a temporary, but significant decrease during the recovery phase of the EXE trial, at 38.5°C ( p < 0.01). The KYN/TRP ratio showed an initial significant increase in the EXE trial ( p < 0.01) that returned to baseline, while in the EXO trial, the ratio appeared to be significantly elevated when participants returned to baseline temperature ( p < 0.05; Figure 4H ). Both trials brought about an increase in plasma KYNA levels, reaching their peak during the recovery phase at 38.5°C ( p < 0.0001 for EXE and p < 0.05 for EXO). The increase was more evident in the EXE trial (increasing from 52.9 nM to 83.7 nM) as compared to the EXO trial (increasing from 52.6 to 65.7 nM). Plasma QUIN levels increased during both trials, reaching similar levels and peaking at 39°C and 38.5°C (recovery phase) for EXE and EXO, respectively ( p < 0.05). In the EXE trial, the QUIN/KYNA ratio gradually declined during the heating and recovery phases, with partial recovery occurring before the return to baseline temperature, whereas in the EXO trial, it remained largely unchanged (Figure 4I ). Plasma 3‐HK and PIC levels were only affected in the EXE trial. For both metabolites, a steady increase of plasma levels was observed during the heating phase, but the effects were more pronounced during the recovery phase, reaching peak concentrations at 38°C ( p < 0.001 for both). Lastly, plasma NAM concentrations were affected by both trials. While NAM levels in the EXE trial decreased during the recovery phase ( p < 0.01), plasma NAM levels in the EXO trial decreased during the heating phase ( p < 0.05) and recovered back to baseline as soon as the participants entered the recovery phase. PIC and NAM are the only metabolites whose values were different between the post‐intervention trials ( p < 0.05 and p < 0.01, respectively). Regarding the EXE trial, all metabolites except KYNA and PIC had similar post‐intervention levels to baseline ( p < 0.01 and p < 0.001, respectively). Correlation analysis revealed that noradrenaline and adrenaline generally exhibited similar patterns of correlation with KP metabolites in both trials, whereas cortisol did not. At baseline and the heating phase of the EXE trial, negative correlations were observed between most KP metabolites and stress markers, while the KYN/TRP ratio positively correlated with adrenaline and noradrenaline (Figure S1 ). However, those correlations were lost in the recovery phase of the EXE trial. The most notable difference between EXO and EXE, based on the correlation analysis, is the significant positive correlation between KYNA and cortisol identified at 39°C during the EXO trial. 4 Discussion The present study successfully addressed its primary aim of exploring the impact of two heating modalities, EXE and EXO, on physiological parameters, stress markers, and plasma concentrations of KP metabolites in healthy males. The findings provide support for the initial hypothesis that the peripheral KP is responsive to heat stress, exhibiting transient induction followed by a rapid return to homeostatic levels. While both EXO and EXE trials activate the SNS and HPA via heat stress, the EXE trial also produces exercise stress, leading to different effects on stress markers like catecholamines and cortisol. As anticipated, all stress markers exhibited a greater increase in the EXE trial compared to the EXO trial (Figure 3F–H ). Distinct response patterns are observed when these markers are divided into the SNS component (adrenaline and noradrenaline) and the HPA component (cortisol). The gradual rise in cortisol concentrations followed the overall increase in KP metabolites, reaching peak concentrations in the recovery phase. In contrast, the SNS‐related markers displayed a more pronounced and rapid elevation during the heating phase (Figure 3F,G ), reflecting the rapid onset of sympathetic activation. These findings align with the established fact that the SNS triggers immediate stress responses, while the HPA axis operates on a slower timescale, as also indicated in our correlation analyses between catecholamines and the KP metabolites versus cortisol and the KP metabolites (Figure S1 ). Additionally, while negative correlations between KP metabolites and stress markers (mostly cortisol) were observed at baseline and the start of the EXE trial, they were lost during the recovery phase. Interestingly, despite the absence of correlations between individual KP metabolites and catecholamines, a positive association was observed between the KYN/TRP ratio and catecholamines. Overall, this suggests that the changes in KP metabolite levels are not directly related to the stress marker levels.

Overall, this suggests that the changes in KP metabolite levels are not directly related to the stress marker levels. The KP of tryptophan degradation has been proven to be highly induced by physiological and psychological stressors, as well as by cytokine release [ 1 , 9 , 38 ]. Upon induction, several neuroactive metabolites, such as KYNA, QUIN, and PIC, are produced. They affect glutamatergic and dopaminergic signaling and are implicated in a variety of diseases, such as neurological, psychiatric, cardiovascular disorders, and cancer [ 39 ]. While there is a plethora of evidence of an involvement of the KP in several diseases, its regulation under healthy conditions and during physiological stress remains insufficiently explored [ 3 , 9 ]. The results of the present study reveal an induction of the KP during EXE heating (in the form of cycling exercise), as most metabolites as well as the KYN/TRP ratio showed significant increases, while NAM decreased (Figure 4 ). It is noteworthy that concentrations of most metabolites were steadily increasing during the heating phase of the EXE trial and then reached their peak concentrations during the recovery phase of the trial. Importantly, all metabolite concentrations, except KYNA and PIC, reverted to their baseline levels upon returning to homeostatic temperatures. This is in line with the fact that these are end‐products of the KP and their main elimination route is relatively slow by excretion in urine [ 40 , 41 ]. Conversely to EXE, only plasma KYNA and QUIN levels increased during the EXO trial, while NAM decreased during the heating phase. These effects were dependent on water temperature, and therefore unlikely to result from water immersion alone. This disparity in activation strength is likely because the EXE trial induces greater sympathetic vasomotor activity than the EXO trial, primarily due to the muscle strain associated with cycling, as reflected by increased plasma adrenaline concentration.

Evidence shows that physical exercise benefits both health and disease, as patients with depression also experience symptom improvements through regular exercise [ 42 ]. In the context of exercise benefits on health, the kynurenine pathway has been investigated. Different types of exercise have been employed across those studies—ranging from marathon racing to cycling and resistance exercise [ 8 , 9 , 32 , 43 , 44 , 45 ]. While most studies have not reported any differences in plasma TRP levels, downstream metabolites were seen to be more affected. The change in plasma KYN, KYNA and QUIN levels following exercise seems to be dependent on the type of exercise, as both increased and decreased levels have been reported. While 30 min of cycling increased plasma KYN and KYNA levels in healthy or type 2 diabetes patients [ 43 ], 45 min of cycling did not affect KYN levels but increased KYNA and QUIN levels in plasma [ 44 ]. Moreover, an increase in plasma KYNA levels has also been reported upon running or cycling endurance activities [ 32 , 45 ]. Consistent with previous studies, increased plasma KYNA levels during EXE trial were also observed in this study (Figure 4C,I ). Since exercise stimulates peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptor‐gamma coactivator 1‐alpha (PGC‐1α) expression in skeletal muscle and increases KAT enzyme expression, peripheral KYNA levels would be expected to increase [ 32 , 46 , 47 ]. PGC‐1α is also known to induce the expression of 2‐amino‐3‐carboxymuconate‐6‐semialdehyde decarboxylase (ACMSD) [ 48 ], which is the enzyme responsible for PIC production. Increased PIC concentration also suggests elevated acetyl‐CoA synthesis, which feeds into the tricarboxylic acid cycle generating energy. In line with this evidence, this study showed elevated plasma PIC levels during the EXE trial. Among all metabolites measured, NAM stands out as the only one decreasing in the heating phase of the EXO trial and returning to normal as soon as recovery begins (Figure 4G ). In contrast, in the EXE trial, NAM levels remained suppressed during the recovery phase. In contrast, in the EXE trial, NAM levels remained suppressed during the recovery phase. Given the intimate connection between NAM and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD + ), it is likely the latter, generated via the kynurenine pathway, may influence NAM levels. Such an idea is consistent with recent evidence showing that acute exercise increases the gene expression and protein abundance of several key NAD + metabolic enzymes [ 49 ]. Further, a tentative contribution by stimulation of the aryl hydrocarbon receptor by the excess of KYNA should not be disregarded when interpreting the present results, as this receptor could further modulate NAD + metabolism and consequently NAM availability. 5 Limitations Despite the small sample size, the cross‐over design employed in the study enhances the strength of the results presented. This study focused exclusively on young individuals and did not include female participants, which limits the generalizability of the findings, as both age and sex influence heat tolerance. Additionally, while a slight difference in room temperature between the two trials was necessary and unavoidable, it should be acknowledged. 6 Conclusion, Future Research and Implications In conclusion, the present study provides evidence on the induction of the KP upon different physiological heat stress modalities and gives insights regarding changes in KP metabolites and their potential implications for health and disease. While KP metabolites and stress markers are affected upon heat stress, their fluctuations throughout the trials seem to be independent of each other. This research enhances our understanding of how the pathway may be regulated in healthy states and its implications for disease while also highlighting the potential of these metabolites as disease biomarkers. When integrated with existing research on the pathway's involvement in infectious disease and conditions like schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, this knowledge deepens our understanding of its broader significance in human health.
